## Introduction

This tutorial covers [Git](https://git-scm.com/), a program for keeping track of changes in your code, and [GitHub](https://github.com/), the leading platform for storing your code in the cloud. Some material is from [*R for Data Science (2e)*](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/) by Hadley Wickham, Mine Çetinkaya-Rundel, and Garrett Grolemund. 

The most useful references for Git/GitHub are [*Happy Git and GitHub for the useR*](https://happygitwithr.com/) and [*Pro Git*](https://git-scm.com/book/en/v2). Refer to these for questions and further learning. Or use AI!

## Using Git

GitHub is an online drive for all your R code and projects. In the professional world, what you have in your GitHub account is often more important than what you have on your resume.

Until now, `connect-repo` has done the GitHub setup for you. This section shows what it did, one setting at a time, by comparing two Codespaces. In one, your usual one, `connect-repo` has run. In the other, it has not. For each setting you will look at the raw Codespace, look at your usual one, and then make the raw one match by hand.

[Git](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Git) is "software for tracking changes in any set of files, usually used for coordinating work among programmers collaboratively developing source code during software development."

### Exercise 6

In the raw Codespace, run `gh auth status`. Copy the output and paste it here.

```{r}
#| label: using-git-28
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "In the raw Codespace, run gh auth status. Copy the output and paste it here.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{.output}
codespace-starter $ gh auth status
github.com
  ✓ Logged in to github.com account your-username (GITHUB_TOKEN)
  - Active account: true
  - Git operations protocol: https
  - Token: ghu_************************************
  - Token scopes: none
```

###

`gh` is GitHub's command-line program. `git` tracks changes and has never heard of GitHub. `gh` talks to github.com.

The parentheses say where the login came from: `GITHUB_TOKEN`, a token GitHub placed in the environment when it built the machine. That token acts as the Codespace, not as you. It can read `codespace-starter` and nothing else, and it cannot create a repo.

### Exercise 8

In the raw Codespace, run these three commands, one at a time:

```bash
unset GITHUB_TOKEN
echo 'unset GITHUB_TOKEN' >> ~/.bashrc
gh auth login --hostname github.com --git-protocol https --web --clipboard=false
```

For the login, `gh` first asks `Authenticate Git with your GitHub credentials? (Y/n)`. Press `Enter`. It then shows a one-time code and says `Press Enter to open https://github.com/login/device in your browser...`. Press `Enter`, paste the code into the GitHub tab that opens, and come back to the Terminal.

Then run `gh auth status`. Copy the output and paste it here.

```{r}
#| label: using-git-29
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "In the raw Codespace, run unset GITHUB_TOKEN, then echo 'unset GITHUB_TOKEN' >> ~/.bashrc, then gh auth login --hostname github.com --git-protocol https --web --clipboard=false, following the prompts. Then run gh auth status. Copy the output and paste it here.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{.output}
codespace-starter $ gh auth status
github.com
  ✓ Logged in to github.com account your-username (/home/rstudio/.config/gh/hosts.yml)
  - Active account: true
  - Git operations protocol: https
  - Token: gho_************************************
  - Token scopes: 'gist', 'read:org', 'repo', 'workflow'
```

###

The first command removes the built-in token from this terminal, so `gh` looks for a real login. The second removes it from every terminal you open later. The third signs you in. On this setting, the raw Codespace now matches yours.

`gh` knows who you are now. `git` does not ask `gh`. When `git push` needs a password it looks in its own places, and this file is the one that matters. Without it, a push from this Codespace goes out as the built-in token or stops at `Username for 'https://github.com':`.

### Exercise 10

In your `github-introduction` Codespace, run `ls -l ~/.git-credentials`. CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: using-git-31
#| echo: false

  "In your github-introduction Codespace, run ls -l ~/.git-credentials. CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",

)
```

###

```{.output}
github-introduction $ ls -l ~/.git-credentials
-rw------- 1 rstudio rstudio 75 Oct 23 09:12 /home/rstudio/.git-credentials
```

###

`connect-repo` wrote your token into this file. `-rw-------` means only you can read it. Every push from this Codespace, from the Terminal or from the Source Control pane, reads it and goes out as you. Never `cat` this file where anyone can see your screen.

### Exercise 11

In the raw Codespace, run these four commands, one at a time:

```bash
git config --global --replace-all credential.helper ""
git config --global --add credential.helper store
printf 'https://x-access-token:%s@github.com\n' "$(gh auth token)" > ~/.git-credentials
chmod 600 ~/.git-credentials
```

Then run `ls -l ~/.git-credentials`. Copy the output and paste it here.

```{r}
#| label: using-git-32
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "In the raw Codespace, run git config --global --replace-all credential.helper \"\", then git config --global --add credential.helper store, then printf 'https://x-access-token:%s@github.com\\n' \"$(gh auth token)\" > ~/.git-credentials, then chmod 600 ~/.git-credentials. Then run ls -l ~/.git-credentials. Copy the output and paste it here.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{.output}
codespace-starter $ ls -l ~/.git-credentials
-rw------- 1 rstudio rstudio 75 Oct 23 14:30 /home/rstudio/.git-credentials
```

###

The first command clears any password helpers the Codespace came with. The second tells Git to use a file. The third writes your token into it: `gh auth token` prints the token and `>` sends it to the file. `chmod 600` makes the file readable by you alone.

```bash
cd /workspaces
gh repo create scratch-repo --public --clone
```

Then run `ls`. Copy the output and paste it here.

```{r}
#| label: using-git-7
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "In the raw Codespace, run cd /workspaces, then gh repo create scratch-repo --public --clone. Then run ls. Copy the output and paste it here.",
  type = "reflection",

```

###

```{.output}
codespace-starter $ cd /workspaces
workspaces $ gh repo create scratch-repo --public --clone
✓ Created repository your-username/scratch-repo on github.com
  https://github.com/your-username/scratch-repo
workspaces $ ls
codespace-starter  scratch-repo
workspaces $
```

###

One command did two jobs. It created the repo on GitHub, and `--clone` made a local folder wired to it. Every repo you have made in this course was born this way, which is why `ls /workspaces` in your `github-introduction` Codespace shows `github-introduction` beside the launcher.

### Exercise 13

How does the local folder know which GitHub repo it belongs to? In the raw Codespace, run:

```bash
cd scratch-repo
git remote -v
git log
```

Copy the output and paste it here.

```{r}
#| label: using-git-8
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "In the raw Codespace, run cd scratch-repo, then git remote -v, then git log. Copy the output and paste it here.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{.output}
workspaces $ cd scratch-repo
scratch-repo $ git remote -v
origin  https://github.com/your-username/scratch-repo.git (fetch)
origin  https://github.com/your-username/scratch-repo.git (push)
scratch-repo $ git log
fatal: your current branch 'main' does not have any commits yet
scratch-repo $
```

###

`origin` is Git's nickname for the copy of your repo on GitHub. Pushes go to `origin` and pulls come from it. When a push goes wrong, `git remote -v` is the first thing to check, because it shows where Git thinks your work is going. The URL ends in `.git`. Drop that and you have the repo's web page.

`git log` refuses outright because `main` has no commits yet. The "fatal" does not mean anything is broken.

### Exercise 14

Still in `scratch-repo` in the raw Codespace, run `ls -a`. The `a` option shows hidden files, whose names start with a dot. Copy the output and paste it here.

```{r}
#| label: using-git-35
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Still in scratch-repo in the raw Codespace, run ls -a. Copy the output and paste it here.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{.output}
scratch-repo $ ls -a
.  ..  .git
scratch-repo $
```

###

`.` is this directory and `..` is its parent. `.git` is the hidden directory where Git keeps every version of every file. Never edit anything inside it. A repo made by `gh repo create` holds nothing else.

### Exercise 17

We do not need `scratch-repo`. In the raw Codespace, try to delete it from the command line. Run `gh repo delete scratch-repo`. Copy whatever happens, including a refusal, and paste it here.

```{r}
#| label: using-git-9
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "In the raw Codespace, run gh repo delete scratch-repo. Copy whatever happens, including a refusal, and paste it here.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{.output}
scratch-repo $ gh repo delete scratch-repo
? Type your-username/scratch-repo to confirm deletion: your-username/scratch-repo
HTTP 403: Must have admin rights to Repository. (https://api.github.com/repos/your-username/scratch-repo)
This API operation needs the "delete_repo" scope. To request it, run:  gh auth refresh -h github.com -s delete_repo
scratch-repo $
```

![](images/gh-repo-delete.png){width=90%}

`gh` first makes you type the repo's full name. Only after you confirm does GitHub refuse. Your exact message may differ.

###

Look back at the token scopes from Exercise 7. `delete_repo` was not among them. Deleting a repository destroys its history, its issues, and its published site, so your everyday credentials deliberately lack the power. You could grant it with the `gh auth refresh` command shown. Don't. The normal way to delete a repo is the website, which forces you to slow down.

### Exercise 18

Delete `scratch-repo` from the website. Go to its page on GitHub (`https://github.com/your-username/scratch-repo`), click **Settings** in the top menu, and scroll to the bottom, to the **Danger Zone**. Click **Delete this repository** and follow the prompts. GitHub makes you type the repository's full name to confirm.

Then, in the raw Codespace, confirm it is gone and remove the local clone. Run these commands, one at a time:

```bash
cd /workspaces
gh repo view scratch-repo
rm -rf scratch-repo
ls
```

Copy the output and paste it here.

```{r}
#| label: using-git-10
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Delete scratch-repo from its Settings page on GitHub (Danger Zone, Delete this repository). Then, in the raw Codespace, run cd /workspaces, then gh repo view scratch-repo, then rm -rf scratch-repo, then ls. Copy the output and paste it here.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{.output}
scratch-repo $ cd /workspaces
workspaces $ gh repo view scratch-repo
GraphQL: Could not resolve to a Repository with the name 'your-username/scratch-repo'. (repository)
workspaces $ rm -rf scratch-repo
workspaces $ ls
codespace-starter
workspaces $
```

###

The Danger Zone's type-the-full-name step is friction by design. You will delete repos fairly often, and the control is always at **Settings**, bottom of the page. Deleting the repo on GitHub did not delete the local clone. The filing cabinet and the desk are separate, so you removed the folder yourself. The same is true in reverse: deleting a local folder never touches GitHub.

### Exercise 20

Create a new Quarto document. From the three horizontal bar icon in the Activity Bar, select `File -> New File...`, then select `Quarto Document` from the drop-down menu. This opens the new file in the Editor.

![](images/create-analysis.png){width=90%}

The new file has no name yet, so its Editor tab reads `Untitled-1`, with a black dot showing that it has never been saved.

Change the title to "Analysis 1" and add your name as the author. Save the file with `Cmd/Ctrl + S`. Because the file is new, VS Code shows a Save As box with a path field. Make sure the path ends in `github-introduction/analysis-1.qmd` and press **OK**.

![](images/save-as-dialog.png){width=90%}

![](images/save-analysis.png){width=90%}

After saving, the tab reads `analysis-1.qmd` and is green with a "U": the file is saved, but **U**ntracked by Git. (The Codespace auto-saves after a short delay, so from now on the black dot appears only briefly as you type.)

Then run `cat analysis-1.qmd`.

CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: using-git-11
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Create a new Quarto document. From the three horizontal bar icon in the Activity Bar, select File -> New File..., then select Quarto Document from the drop-down menu. This opens the new file in the Editor. Change the title to \"Analysis 1\" and add your name as the author. Save the file with Cmd/Ctrl + S. Because the file is new, VS Code shows a Save As box with a path field. Make sure the path ends in github-introduction/analysis-1.qmd and press OK. Then run cat analysis-1.qmd. CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

You should have something like this:

```{.output}
github-introduction $ cat analysis-1.qmd 
---
title: "Analysis 1"
author: "PPBDS Student"
format: html
---

github-introduction $
```

The file is nothing but a YAML header. Quarto's template supplies a title, an author, and an output format, and you supplied the values.

### Exercise 21

Click the Source Control button in the Activity Bar. This opens the Source Control pane, which is an interface to using Git and GitHub.

![](images/analysis-git.png){width=90%}

The top part of the pane shows the files that have been added or modified. Again, the "U" at the end of the lines for `AGENTS.md` and `analysis-1.qmd` indicates that Git has noticed these files but that they are **U**ntracked.

Render `analysis-1.qmd` with `Cmd/Ctrl + Shift + K`.

Three things happen. A new terminal named **Quarto Preview** appears in the Panel and fills with output. A **Quarto Preview** tab opens in the Editor beside your file, showing the rendered HTML. And VS Code pops up a notice that your application is running on port NNNN, with an **Open in Browser** button. Ignore the notice.

![](images/analysis-preview.png){width=90%}

Copy/paste the last few lines from the Quarto Preview terminal.

Your answer should look like:

```{.output}
metadata
```

```{.output}
clipboard.min.js

anchor.min.js  popper.min.js  quarto.js  quarto-syntax-highlighting-bf27225e3a48a9273f3daa8f8e829971.css  tabsets  tippy.css  tippy.umd.min.js

analysis-1_files/libs/quarto-html/tabsets:
tabsets.js
github-introduction $ 
```

Whenever you render a document using Quarto, it creates a directory called `base-name-of-your-file_files`. Since the base name of `analysis-1.qmd` is `analysis-1`, the new directory is `analysis-1_files`. It holds the support files --- scripts, style sheets, fonts --- that `analysis-1.html` loads in the browser. We usually don't want it monitored by Git or stored on GitHub.

The button says **Publish Branch** rather than **Sync Changes** because this is the repo's very first push: GitHub does not yet have a `main` branch to sync with. After this one push the button will read **Sync Changes** with a count of the commits waiting to go out.

The bottom portion of the pane, the Source Control Graph, shows the Git history of this repo. It lists your commits, newest on top, each marked only with `main`. There is no cloud icon anywhere, because nothing has reached GitHub yet. (The picture was taken after a single commit. You have two.)

### Exercise 32

Press the **Publish Branch** button.

###

The Source Control View should now look like this:

![](images/analysis-1-post-sync.png){width=90%}

The button is gone, and a purple cloud icon has appeared on the most recent commit, beside the local `main` branch. The cloud represents the remote tracking branch on GitHub, called `origin/main`: the `main` branch on the `origin` repo, which is the GitHub repo. Until now there was no such thing.

From the bash Terminal, run `git log` again. CP/CR.


Your answer should look like:

```{.output}
github-introduction $ git log
commit 4c0f3f9d2b7e1a6c5d8e9f0a1b2c3d4e5f6a7b8c (HEAD -> main, origin/main)
Author: Your Name <your-username@users.noreply.github.com>
Date:   Tue Oct 13 00:07:10 2026 +0000

    added sentence

commit 81f70abb905c2c8d328a919115e18038ab3df006
Author: Your Name <your-username@users.noreply.github.com>
Date:   Tue Oct 13 00:05:06 2026 +0000

    initial version
```

The top line has changed from "(HEAD -> main)" to "(HEAD -> main, origin/main)". Our changes have been pushed to GitHub, not simply committed locally.

The long string after "commit" is the address of that commit. We can use it to revert to the codebase as it looked after that commit.

###

As AI writes more and more of our code, it's becoming increasingly important to get good at managing this code with Git and GitHub.

## Publishing with GitHub Pages

An HTML file rendered by Quarto only lives on your computer (or Codespace) — it isn't accessible to anyone else. [GitHub Pages](https://pages.github.com/) solves this by serving the static files from your GitHub repository as a public website, giving you a real URL you can share with anyone.

GitHub Pages isn't the only option. [Netlify](https://www.netlify.com/), [Quarto Pub](https://quartopub.com/), and [Posit Connect](https://posit.co/products/enterprise/connect/) are some popular alternatives for hosting HTML files and websites.

### Exercise 2

If you click the Source Control button, your Codespaces window should look something like this:

![](images/analysis-1-git-post-graph.png){width=90%}

Commit your files with a message like "beautiful graphic". Once you do, the button reads **Sync Changes 1**, and hovering over it shows "Push 1 commits to origin/main" --- this is not the first push, so GitHub already has a `main` branch to sync with. The Graph now has a third entry, your new commit, marked `main`, while the cloud for `origin/main` still sits on "added sentence".

![](images/analysis-1-post-commit-sync-changes.png){width=90%}

Press **Sync Changes** to push. Don't forget that "push" means the same thing as "sync."

Click the **Quarto Preview** tab in the Panel and use `Ctrl + c` to stop the Quarto watching process. From the bash Terminal, run `git log -n 1`. CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: publishing-with-github-pages-2
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Use Ctrl + c to stop the Quarto watching process. From the bash Terminal, run git log -n 1. CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{.output}
github-introduction $ git log -n 1
commit 42b4257f7223a2ef8af1c6a7399ec777f2b90a3f (HEAD -> main, origin/main)
Author: Your Name <your-username@users.noreply.github.com>
Date:   Tue Oct 13 00:10:30 2026 +0000

    beautiful graphic
github-introduction $
```

We are being a little sloppy to equate "pushing" with "syncing." Strictly speaking, "syncing" does two things: it "pushes" your changes to GitHub *and* it "pulls" any changes made on GitHub to your local computer. But, in this case, because no one else but you can change the GitHub repo, there is nothing to "pull."

Let's publish our results to [GitHub Pages](https://pages.github.com/). Before we do, go to the GitHub repo for `github-introduction`, click on the "Settings" top menu item, and then click on the "Pages" side menu item.

![](images/repo-settings-pages.png){width=90%}

CP/CR just the first 10 or so lines of the output.


```{r}

#| echo: false

  "Go to the GitHub repo for github-introduction, click on the Settings top menu item, and then click on the Pages side menu item. We won't modify these options by hand. From the bash Terminal, run quarto publish gh-pages analysis-1.qmd. Respond with \"Y\" when it asks whether you want to publish. CP/CR just the first 10 or so lines of the output.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE

```

###

Here is what I see, broken up to allow for comments:

```{.output}
github-introduction $ quarto publish gh-pages analysis-1.qmd
? Publish site to https://your-username.github.io/github-introduction/ using gh-pages? (Y/n) › Yes
```

Quarto asks this question on every publish. There is a setting that turns it off.

```{.output}
Switched to a new branch 'gh-pages'
[gh-pages (root-commit) 08825ec] Initializing gh-pages branch
remote: 
remote: Create a pull request for 'gh-pages' on GitHub by visiting:        
remote:      https://github.com/your-username/github-introduction/pull/new/gh-pages        
remote: 
To https://github.com/your-username/github-introduction.git
 * [new branch]      HEAD -> gh-pages
```

By default, `quarto publish` follows the standard GitHub Pages approach of creating a new Git "branch" called `gh-pages`. Branches are lightweight pointers to specific commits. They allow you to isolate work in progress, experiment with new features, and collaborate effectively without affecting the main codebase. Note the `.git` on the end of the address, as in `git remote -v`: this is Git talking to GitHub, not a web page.

```{.output}
Switched to branch 'main'
Your branch is up to date with 'origin/main'.
From https://github.com/your-username/github-introduction
 * branch            gh-pages   -> FETCH_HEAD
Rendering for publish:



processing file: analysis-1.qmd
1/5                  
2/5 [unnamed-chunk-1]
3/5                  
4/5 [unnamed-chunk-2]
5/5                  
output file: analysis-1.knit.md
```

`quarto publish` processes `analysis-1.qmd` in the same way that `quarto preview` or `quarto render` does. Further down, after the `pandoc` and `metadata` blocks, you will see a line reading `fatal: pathspec '.' did not match any files`. It is harmless. The fresh `gh-pages` branch has nothing in it yet for Git to tidy away, and the output carries on to `[✓] Published to https://your-username.github.io/github-introduction/`.

## Summary

This tutorial covered [Git](https://git-scm.com/), a program for keeping track of changes in your code, and [GitHub](https://github.com/), the leading platform for storing your code in the cloud. Some material is from [*R for Data Science (2e)*](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/) by Hadley Wickham, Mine Çetinkaya-Rundel, and Garrett Grolemund.

The most useful reference for Git/GitHub is [*Happy Git and GitHub for the useR*](https://happygitwithr.com/). Refer to that book whenever you have a question.
